# `nish/regex`

Regular expressions whose search time is linear in the input, whatever the pattern.

```ts
import {
  REGEX_MAX_CLASS_RANGES,
  REGEX_MAX_DEPTH,
  REGEX_MAX_GROUPS,
  REGEX_MAX_INSTRUCTIONS,
  REGEX_MAX_PROPERTY_RANGES,
  REGEX_MAX_REPEAT,
  Regex,
  RegexMatch,
  regexCompile,
  regexEscape,
} from "nish/regex";
```

```ts
import { Regex, RegexMatch, regexCompile } from "nish/regex";

const compiled = regexCompile("(?<year>\\d{4})-(?<month>\\d{2})", "")
if (compiled.isErr()) {
  // compiled.error is the reason, such as "regex: missing ) at byte 0"
} else {
  const re: Regex = compiled.value
  const m: RegexMatch = new RegexMatch()
  if (re.exec("due 2026-10", 0, m)) {
    // m.start() 4, m.end() 11, m.named("month") "10"
  }
  re.replaceAll("2026-10 and 2027-01", "$<month>/$<year>")  // "10/2026 and 01/2027"
}
```

<scalar-callout type="info">

**The syntax is JavaScript's**, with the `u` flag's strictness: literals,
`.`, classes `[a-z]` and `[^…]`, `\d \w \s` and their negations, `\b \B ^
$`, groups `(…)`, `(?:…)` and `(?<name>…)`, `|`, and the quantifiers `* + ?
{n} {n,} {n,m}` with their lazy `?` forms. Escapes are `\n \r \t \f \v \0`,
`\cX`, `\xHH`, `\uHHHH`, `\u{H…}` and a backslash before any syntax
character; a `{`, `}` or `]` that does not belong to a quantifier or a
class is an error rather than a literal, so write `\{`. `\p{…}` and
`\P{…}` are Unicode 16.0's properties as JavaScript names them: a
General_Category value (`L`, `Lu`, `Letter`, `gc=Nd`), `Script=` or
`Script_Extensions=` a script (`sc=Grek`, `scx=Deva`), or a binary property
(`Alphabetic`, `Emoji`, `ASCII`, `Any`, `Assigned`). The flags are `i`, `m`
(`^` and `$` at line terminators), `s` (`.` matches them too) and `u`,
which changes nothing. `i` folds A-Z to a-z, and above ASCII follows
Unicode's simple case folding, so `σ` matches `Σ` and `ς` and `[α-ω]` the
capitals; unlike JavaScript nothing folds across ASCII, so the Kelvin sign
and `ſ` match no `k` or `s`, though under `i` both are word characters to
`\w`, `\W`, `\b` and `\B`, as with JavaScript's `iu`.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-callout type="warning">

**Backreferences and
lookaround are refused at compile time**: they are what makes a matcher
backtrack, and this one never does. A repeat count is at most 1,000, a
pattern at most 100,000 instructions once its repeats are written out,
1,024 capturing groups and 10,000 ranges in one class, and its property
escapes and case folding add at most 100,000 ranges to its classes.

</scalar-callout>

<scalar-detail title="Matching never backtracks">

A search runs a lazy DFA first: it builds
its states from the compiled program as the text needs them, so it reads a
byte per step and the leftmost-first match's end comes from a table lookup.
A reverse DFA, run back from that end, finds where the match starts, and a
Pike VM, the construction RE2, Go's `regexp` and Rust's `regex` use, runs
from that start only when a group's capture is wanted. A pattern with a
literal no match can avoid, such as `\w+@example`, is searched for by that
literal and the match grown both ways from it. Every engine follows every
alternative at once, so a match costs O(pattern × input) at worst and
`(a+)+$` against a thousand `a`s and a `b` is as quick as `a+$`. Finding
every match (`findAll`, `count`, `replaceAll`, `split`) is one search per
match, so it is quadratic when a preferred branch reads far ahead before a
short one wins: `<[^>]*>|<` over a text of `<`s rereads the rest of the text
for each, as it does in RE2 and Rust's `regex`. Which match
is found is the one JavaScript finds — the leftmost, and of those the one
the first alternative and the greediest quantifier prefer — and a group
inside a quantifier keeps only its last iteration's capture, as in
JavaScript. An iteration past a quantifier's minimum that matches empty is
rejected, as JavaScript rejects it. The VM keeps one thread per
instruction, position and set of iterations begun, so `(a*?)+?$` on "aa"
captures "a", as JavaScript does; past three such quantifiers nested in one
another the deeper ones share their threads, and a capture there can be a
different iteration's than JavaScript's.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Strings are UTF-8 and offsets are bytes">

**Strings are UTF-8 and offsets are bytes**, like `s.length`. The VM steps
a code point at a time, so `.` and `[^a]` consume a whole character; a byte
that is not part of valid UTF-8 is one character of its own, which no
literal and no range matches. `\w`, `\d` and `\b` are ASCII, as they are in
JavaScript; `\s` is JavaScript's whitespace, U+FEFF and U+3000 included.
After an empty match `findAll`, `replaceAll` and `split` step one character.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="What a call costs">

The VM's two thread lists, its capture tables and
its stack are allocated once by `regexCompile`. `test` tracks no captures,
`findAll` and a `replace` whose template names no group track only the
match's bounds, and only `exec`, `find`, `split` and a template with `$1` or
`$<name>` pay for every group. A pattern that starts with a literal is searched for with
`s.indexOf`; one whose first few bytes are each one of a set rare enough to
be worth it, like `[A-Z][a-z]` or `cat|dog`, is searched for those bytes by
a runtime kernel that tests sixteen or thirty-two starts at a time; any
other whose first characters are known skips the bytes that cannot start a
match with a 128-entry table; and a pattern that is nothing but a literal
never starts an engine at all. The DFA's states are
built as searches need them and kept, so only a search that meets new
states allocates, and only up to a bound:
its table holds at most 2,048 states and 262,144 transitions (1 MiB), and
a search that fills it clears it and goes on; one that keeps clearing it
without reading at least 10 bytes per state hands the rest of the text to
the VM, which is slower but never needs more memory. Because the scratch
memory lives in the `Regex`, one `Regex` is used by one thread at a time.

</scalar-detail>

## regexCompile

Compile `pattern` with `flags`, a string of `i`, `m`, `s` and `u` in any
order; `u` changes nothing, as patterns are always read by code point.
The error names what is wrong and its byte in the pattern.

```ts
function regexCompile(
  pattern: string,
  flags: string,
): Result<Regex, string>
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="pattern" type="string" required>

The pattern, in JavaScript's syntax without the slashes.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="flags" type="string" required>

Any of `i` (ignore case), `m` (`^` and `$` match at line ends), `s` (`.` matches a newline) and `u`, each at most once.

</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Result&lt;Regex, string&gt;">

The compiled pattern, or the reason it does not compile, such as "regex: missing ) at byte 0" or `regex: invalid flags "x"`.

</scalar-field>

## regexEscape

`text` with every syntax character escaped, so that it compiles to a
pattern matching exactly `text`.

```ts
function regexEscape(text: string): string
```

#### Parameters

<scalar-field name="text" type="string" required>

The literal text to match.

</scalar-field>

#### Returns

<scalar-field name="returns" type="string">

A pattern for `regexCompile`; `text` unchanged when it holds no syntax character.

</scalar-field>

## Regex

A compiled pattern: its program, its classes, what the prefilters read and
the VM's scratch memory. Made by `regexCompile`.

```ts
class Regex
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `readonly flags: string` | The flags as written. |
| `groups: i32` | Capture groups, the whole match included. |
| `readonly source: string` | The pattern as written. |
| `count(text: string): i32` | How many matches `findAll` would answer, without making their strings. |
| `exec(text: string, from: i32, m: RegexMatch): boolean` | Search `text` from byte `from` and fill `m` with the first match and every group. Answers whether there was one; `m` is untouched when not. Reusing one `RegexMatch` makes a loop of searches allocate nothing. |
| `find(text: string, from: i32): RegexMatch \| null` | The first match at or after byte `from`. |
| `findAll(text: string): string[]` | The text of every match, left to right, none overlapping. After an empty match the search resumes one character on. |
| `groupCount(): i32` | How many groups the pattern has. |
| `groupIndex(name: string): i32` | The number of a named group. |
| `replace(text: string, replacement: string): string` | `text` with its first match replaced by `replacement`, which is `String.prototype.replace`'s template: `$$` is `$`, `$&` the match, `` $` `` and `$'` the text before and after it, `$1` to `$99` a group and `$<name>` a named one; a group that took no part is "". |
| `replaceAll(text: string, replacement: string): string` | `text` with every match replaced by `replacement`, as `replace` reads it. |
| `split(text: string): string[]` | `text` cut at every match, as `String.prototype.split` cuts it: each group's text follows the piece before its match ("" for one that took no part), an empty match where the last piece ended or at the end cuts nothing, and "" splits to nothing when the pattern matches it, else to `[""]`. |
| `test(text: string): boolean` | Whether the pattern matches anywhere in `text`. |

## RegexMatch

One match: the input it was found in and the byte offsets of every group.

```ts
class RegexMatch
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new RegexMatch()` | An empty match with no groups, for `Regex.exec` to fill in. |
| `end(): i32` | Where the match ends. |
| `group(k: i32): string` | Group `k`'s text. |
| `groupCount(): i32` | How many groups the pattern has. |
| `groupEnd(k: i32): i32` | Where group `k` ends. |
| `groupStart(k: i32): i32` | Where group `k` starts. |
| `matched(k: i32): boolean` | Whether group `k` took part in the match. |
| `named(name: string): string` | The text of a named group. |
| `start(): i32` | Where the match starts. |
| `text(): string` | The matched text. |

## Limits

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="10,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_CLASS_RANGES: i32`

The most ranges one class may list; one more is a compile error.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="250" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_DEPTH: i32`

How deeply groups may nest; a deeper pattern is a compile error.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,024" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_GROUPS: i32`

The most capturing groups a pattern may have, past group 0; one more is a
compile error. A name is checked against each.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="100,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_INSTRUCTIONS: i32`

The most instructions a compiled pattern may have; `regexCompile` refuses a bigger program.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="100,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_PROPERTY_RANGES: i32`

The most ranges the property escapes and case folding of one pattern may
add to its classes; one more is a compile error.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`REGEX_MAX_REPEAT: i32`

The largest count `{n}`, `{n,}` or `{n,m}` may give; a larger one is a compile error.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>
